scope: Bounded primary-source literature and exact-filename search; no additional audio downloaded, no model scoring, no expert contact.

candidate.observed_shape: Two similar short, two-part descending events around 50 to 33 Hz. Biological origin and species remain unresolved.

supported_interpretation: Unidentified low-frequency transient candidates in an already-studied 2004 Bering M2 deployment. Their approximate frequency contour resembles a published sei-whale call family, but this does not establish species, Pacific occurrence, or novelty. Instrument noise is specifically documented for this deployment and must be excluded.

primary_sources.title: Bering Sea Baleen Whale Acoustics, NPRB Final Report F0519
primary_sources.locations: Table1 on printed p7; fin-whale methods on printed p9
primary_sources.findings: M2 recording coverage includes April 26 to July 28, 2004; the table records right, fin and humpback whales. The 2004 M2 deployment received manual fin-whale presence/absence review; automated detection was omitted because instrument electronic noise overlapped call frequencies.
primary_sources.implication: The deployment was already studied. Electronics is a documented alternative source for low-frequency features. This report does not label our exact two offsets.

primary_sources.title: Cooperative Acoustic Monitoring of North Pacific Right Whales, MPLTM493
primary_sources.locations: Table3 printed p16; methods printed pp16–18; results p20
primary_sources.findings: BSM2 April 26 to July 28, 2004 is listed at 80 kHz and 72 m depth. Investigators distinguished right-whale calls from similar low-frequency humpback components using longer temporal patterns and visual/aural review. Their earliest reported right-whale detections were May 23, 2004.
primary_sources.implication: Our May 8 descending transients cannot extend that right-whale record without species evidence. Short shape similarity alone was already recognized as ambiguous.

primary_sources.title: 50 to 30-Hz triplet and singlet down sweep vocalizations produced by sei whales in the western North Atlantic Ocean
primary_sources.findings: 50 to 30 Hz downsweeps were attributed to sei whales through association with established 82 to 34 Hz calls and spatial/temporal tracking.
primary_sources.implication: This contour is not a globally unknown sound type. The study concerns the Atlantic, and its attribution evidence is stronger than our two-window resemblance.

primary_sources.title: NOAA NEFSC Passive Acoustics Branch manual: Baleen Whales
primary_sources.findings: Its sei-whale section describes 50 to 30 Hz downsweeps lasting 0.6–1.94 s and says archival daily presence is assessed using downsweep doublets/triplets.
primary_sources.implication: The duration/frequency resemblance supports expert triage, not automatic species confirmation. Two isolated events approximately 749 s apart are not a demonstrated call doublet.

primary_sources.title: MBARC BERING Raw Audio Data
primary_sources.findings: NOAA describes publicly archived historical Scripps recordings and later conversion to FLAC. The landing-page date range starts September 2004, inconsistent with May 2004 filenames; the original 2007 deployment reports cover April–July 2004.
primary_sources.implication: Use source-specific deployment records and recorder timing to settle dates; a new public archive release does not establish that recordings were unexamined.

exact_record_search.result: No exact-file scientific annotation was located in this bounded indexed-web check.
exact_record_search.limitation: This is not evidence that the offsets were never inspected, privately annotated, or included in an aggregate study. Historical publications generally do not index individual FLAC filenames.

next_review: Compare longer same-file context with documented electronic-noise patterns and known whale call sequences; seek source-specific annotations and acoustic expert assessment before assigning species or an unreported occurrence.
